The original [BERT4Rec paper](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1904.06690) explicitly supplements random masked-item training with samples masking only the final item, reporting improved alignment with next-item prediction. This supports including endpoint examples, but does not establish aggressive endpoint oversampling as superior to random-prefix sampling. Its controlled context-length experiments show dataset dependence: Beauty peaks at maximum length 20, MovieLens-1M at 200; longer histories do not consistently help. Optimal masking proportions also differ substantially across datasets. These findings support tuning context length and mask density rather than assuming more endpoint exposure is universally beneficial.

[Recency-based Sampling of Sequences](https://arxiv.org/html/2207.02643) provides adjacent controlled evidence: intermediate recency weighting outperforms endpoint-only sequence continuation across substantial parameter ranges. However, those interventions train SASRec, GRU4Rec and Caser; BERT4Rec serves as a baseline. RSS also samples multiple targets, so it is not a direct BERT4Rec endpoint-versus-random-prefix comparison. Its results motivate testing graded recency sampling, without establishing its superiority within BERT4Rec.

No directly matched controlled study was identified that isolates BERT4Rec endpoint oversampling versus random prefixes while holding context length, target exposure and compute constant, or demonstrates endpoint-induced memorization. The [replicability study](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2207.07483) instead identifies insufficient training as a major confounder. Endpoint oversampling therefore remains a plausible hypothesis. A useful single-model ablation would compare random masking, random-prefix terminal masking and their endpoint-enriched variant, controlling updates and target counts and reporting validation accuracy by history length alongside training–validation gaps.
